entities.name: Temple of Apollo Sosianus
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Temple of Apollo Sosianus in Rome (also known as Temple of Apollo Medicus), one of Rome's oldest Apolline temples (originally founded c. 431 BCE, the second temple built to Apollo in Rome), rebuilt magnificently by Gaius Sosius (consul 32 BCE) using Greek spoils — including Greek sculptures looted from conquered territories — is notable as one of the few surviving Republican-era temple structures in Rome with three standing columns still visible today in the Campo Marzio.

The temple was significant in the context of late Republican and Augustan Rome as a monument of cultural appropriation: Sosius's rebuilding incorporated Greek sculptures (including a 5th-century BCE work attributed to the workshop of Pheidias depicting Heracles) into an explicitly Roman religious monument, demonstrating Rome's pattern of absorbing Greek culture while asserting Roman dominance. Augustus associated Apollo particularly closely with himself (the Battle of Actium was on the Apolline cape Actium), and the Apollo Sosianus temple sat within the Campus Martius near his own Mausoleum.

Archaeologically, the Temple of Apollo Sosianus is valuable because its three standing Corinthian columns (from Sosius's c. 33-20 BCE reconstruction) preserve some of the most complete surviving examples of Late Republican temple architecture. The sculptural program of the pediment (fragments in the Capitoline Museums) depicted a Triumphal procession — one of the most detailed representations of a Roman triumph in sculpture — making it a key document for Roman iconographic programs.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Temple of Apollo Sosianus — preserving three of Rome's few standing Republican-era temple columns, housing pediment sculptures that are the most detailed depiction of a Roman triumph, and demonstrating Roman cultural appropriation of Greek art — is a key archaeological monument for understanding Late Republican Rome.
